explanations.10: This makes the script exit immediately if any command fails, instead of continuing to the next line — it's a safety feature.
explanations.11: This makes the script fail if you try to use a variable that was never set, catching typos and missing setup.
explanations.12: This makes the script fail if any command in a pipeline (commands connected with |) fails, not just the last one.
explanations.14: This sets WORKSPACE to the value of the environment variable ANYTHINGLLM_WORKSPACE, but if that variable doesn't exist, it defaults to 'blog'.
explanations.20: The $* means 'combine all the arguments passed to this script into one string' — so if you run the script with multiple words, they become one question.
explanations.24: This extracts the API key from a .env file by finding the line that starts with ANYTHINGLLM_API_KEY=, taking only the first match, grabbing everything after the equals sign, and removing any quote characters.
explanations.26: The :? syntax means 'if this variable is empty, stop the script and show this error message' — it's a required-variable check.
explanations.30: This attempts to contact the AnythingLLM server at each candidate URL; if the ping succeeds, the loop breaks and saves that URL.
explanations.49: The ${RANDOM}${RANDOM}-$$ creates a unique session ID by combining two random numbers and the script's process ID, ensuring each API call gets its own conversation thread.
explanations.52: This extracts the error field from the JSON response, or outputs nothing (empty) if the field doesn't exist.
explanations.63: [[ -t 1 ]] checks whether the script's output is connected to a terminal; -t 1 means 'is file descriptor 1 (stdout) a terminal?'
explanations.65: The \033] sequences are escape codes that create clickable hyperlinks in modern terminals; the 8;; and \\ brackets mark the start and end of the link.
explanations.74: The .sources[]? means 'get all items from the sources array, or skip this entire section if sources doesn't exist' — the ? prevents errors if sources is missing.
explanations.76: The startswith filter checks if chunkSource begins with 'link://' — only links (not local files) get included in the sources list.
explanations.82: IFS=$'\t' sets the field separator to a tab character, so the read command splits each line at tabs into separate url and title variables.
explanations.83: The ${url##*/} deletes everything up to the last slash, leaving just the filename — used for display as a short label.
explanations.112: mapfile -t reads input into an array, and the process substitution <(...) lets you feed it a pipeline; -t means 'strip newlines from each line'.
explanations.113: tr converts characters: '[:upper:]' to '[:lower:]' changes uppercase to lowercase, and awk filters to keep only words 4 characters or longer.
explanations.114: This uses process substitution to create a temporary file of stopwords, then grep -vxF removes any candidate words that match a stopword exactly.
explanations.120: This divides the total blog post count by 10 to set a ceiling — if a word appears in more than 10% of posts, it's too common to be useful.
explanations.121: [[ ... ]] || means 'if this condition is false, run the next line' — so ceiling becomes 3 at minimum.
explanations.128: The || true at the end means 'if grep finds nothing and exits with an error, ignore that error and let count be 0 instead'.
explanations.141: sed 's/^"//; s/"$//' removes a quote from the start (^) and end ($) of the string — sed is used here because titles might contain colons, unlike awk -F.
explanations.143: This constructs a blog URL from the site base URL, 'blog/' path, and the slug, then passes it to print_source which handles formatting based on terminal type.
